<b>1745</b>Ewald von Kleist y Pieter van: 1745Ewald von Kleist and Pieter van Musschenbroek independently invent the Leyden jar, the first capacitor: two conductors separated by an insulator that store charge.
<b>1848</b>William Thomson, el futuro Lo: 1848William Thomson, the future Lord Kelvin, invents the method of images: the field of a charge next to a conducting plane is that of the charge and an "image" of opposite sign on the other side.
<b>1891</b>La primera línea trifásica de: 1891The first three-phase high-voltage line carries electricity from Lauffen to Frankfurt, 175 km away, at more than 15,000 V. Since then, lines carry energy as alternating current at high voltage.
<b>2004</b>El artista Richard Box clava: 2004The artist Richard Box plants 1,301 fluorescent tubes in a field under a high-voltage line, near Bristol. At dusk they light up on their own with the electric field of the line.
Por el método de las imágenes, el cable: By the method of images, the cable above the conducting ground is the same as two infinite parallel wires with opposite charges, the cable and its image, separated by 2h. The potential and the field come from adding those of the two wires.
Se abre con los dos hilos en el SI, a 10: It opens with the two wires in SI, 10 m above and below the ground and with ±1.028 µC/m. We get a potential difference of 133 kV between the cable and the ground, a field of 3.7 kV/m at the ground and 3.8 kV/m at 1.5 m height, and 4.5 kV between the ends of the fluorescent tube.

Las líneas que cruzan el campo llevan tr: The lines crossing the countryside carry three cables, one per phase. On a 230 kV one, that is the voltage between two cables; between each cable and the ground there is $230/√3 ≈ 133 "kV"$.\n\nIt is 50 Hz alternating current: the voltage of each cable rises and falls, and changes sign, a hundred times per second. At the lowest point of the curve, the cable is about 10 m from the ground.
El cable y el suelo forman un condensado: The cable and the ground form a capacitor
of capacitance per metre of cable.
El suelo húmedo conduce, así que el cabl: Damp ground conducts, so the cable and the ground are two conductors separated by air: a capacitor. If the cable has charge $+λ$ per metre, a negative charge appears by induction in the ground below. To calculate it the method of images is used: the ground is replaced by an image cable with $−λ$ 10 m below. With a cable of radius $a = 1.5 "cm"$ at $h = 10 "m"$: $C′ = {2πε_0}/{ln(2h/a)} = {2π · 8.85 · 10^{−12}}/{ln(1333)} ≈ 7.7 "pF/m"$
Una carga que va y viene: A charge going back and forth
de carga en el cable, que cambia de sign: of charge on the cable, which changes sign 100 times per second.
La carga del cable es $λ = C′ V = 7,7 \": The charge on the cable is $λ = C′ V = 7.7 "pF/m" · 133 "kV" ≈ 1.03 "µC/m"$. Since the voltage is alternating, so is the charge: that of the cable and that of the ground change sign at the same time, 50 times per second in each direction.\n\nWith hundreds of kilometres of line, that charge coming and going is an appreciable current even though nobody uses energy: it is the capacitive current of the line.
El campo eléctrico bajo la línea: The electric field under the line
de campo eléctrico en el suelo, justo de: of electric field on the ground, just below the cable.
Las líneas de campo salen del cable y ac:
The field lines leave the cable and end on the ground, perpendicular to it. Just below, the fields of the cable and of its image point the same way and add up:

$E = 2 · {λ}/{2πε_0 h} = {λ}/{πε_0 h} = {1.03 · 10^{−6}}/{π · 8.85 · 10^{−12} · 10} ≈ 3.7 "kV/m"$

Between the feet and the head of a 1.8 m person there are about 6.7 kV, which change sign with the alternating current. You do not notice them because your body conducts and distorts the field around it.
Un fluorescente que se enciende solo: A fluorescent tube that lights up by itself
entre los extremos de un tubo de 1,2 m s: between the ends of a 1.2 m tube held upright.
Un tubo fluorescente de 1,2 m sostenido:
A 1.2 m fluorescent tube held vertically, with its lower end half a metre from the ground, has between its ends:

$ΔV = λ/(2πε_0) · [ln{h + y}/{h − y}]_{0.5}^{1.7} ≈ 4.5 "kV"$

That is enough to ionise the gas in the tube. Since the voltage is alternating, the charge goes back and forth through the gas a hundred times per second and the tube glows, with no cables or socket.

In 2004 the artist Richard Box planted 1,301 tubes in a field under a line near Bristol: they lit up on their own at dusk.
de corriente por el cuerpo de alguien de: of current through the body of someone standing below: about 20 times less than what is noticeable.
Por tu cuerpo, de pie bajo la línea, pas: Through your body, standing under the line, a capacitive current of about 15 µA per kV/m of field flows to the ground: about 50 µA here. An alternating current begins to be noticed at around 1 mA.\n\nThe European Union recommends not exceeding 5 kV/m where the public is, and that is why the cables are at that height. What can give a shock is touching something large, metallic and insulated from the ground, such as a car or a long fence: it picks up more charge and the whole discharge passes through your hand.
